YEARS of
Celebrating 
50 Years of Motherson. 
Fifty years ago, Motherson began as a small silver trading business. 
In 1983, we took our first step into the automotive industry – with 
one product, one customer, and a clear ambition: to grow by creat -
ing value for all stakeholders through trusted partnerships. Since 
then, we have expanded across continents and diversified into mul-
tiple industries, evolving into a global solutions provider – while 
staying true to the values that shaped our beginning. This journey 
has been made possible by the continued trust of our customers, 
partners, and investors, the commitment of our people, and the be-
lief that together, we go further. As we mark this truly special mile-
stone, we look ahead with the same clarity of purpose and commit -
ment that have brought us here.

5 annual report  2024-2025chapter 2 theme of this year 
This year’s annual report theme – Great 
achievements come to teams who 
collectively believe in their dreams  – 
captures a simple but powerful truth: long-
term success of an organisation doesn’t 
come from the work of any one individual. 
It’s the result of people united around a 
shared vision and belief in their dreams. 
This spirit has been the foundation of 
Motherson for the past 50 years. When  
we started in 1975, our beginnings were 
modest – with INR 1,000, a simple dream, 
and a few people willing to work hard and 
support one another. Today, we’ve grown 
into a group that operates in over 44 
countries, with more than 425 facilities, 
and a team of over 200,000 people. This 
incredible journey has been made possible 
step by step – moving forward together,  
as one team. As we look ahead, we’re not just building 
on our legacy in the automotive industry, 
but also expanding steadily into non-
automotive sectors, including Aerospace, 
Health & Medical, Logistics Solutions, 
Technology & Industrial Solutions. These 
ventures bring challenges, but they also 
unlock exciting opportunities. And our 
teams around the world have already 
established strong foundations in these 
areas. These areas bring fresh challenges, 
but also open doors to new possibilities. 
And with every step forward, we remain 
guided by the same commitment: to do 
more for our customers, together. 
At Motherson, success has never been  
just about big numbers or bold targets. It 
has always been about our people. From 
the shop floors to the boardrooms, from 
long term team members to those who just 
joined, each person contributes to making 
Motherson what it is. We are a community 
that stands by one another through  
ups and downs, remains curious, stays 
committed, and focuses on delivering 
excellence to our customers. 
 As we move forward, we hold on to our 
shared purpose, keep lifting each other  
up, and continue this extraordinary journey 
with faith and perseverance. Together, 
we’ve built something meaningful – a 
company we’re proud to be part of. And  
as long as we continue to move forward  
as one team, one family, we will keep 
making progress—towards new goals,  
new possibilities, and achieve our vision  
for 2030 and beyond. 
When we dream together, we achieve 
together. That’s the Motherson way.

samvardhana motherson international limited6chapter 3 chairman’s letter
Dear 
Shareholders,
FY2024–25 has been a landmark year in  
the Motherson journey, one defined by 
resilience, strategic growth, and record-
breaking performance amid a complex 
global environment. We have delivered our 
strongest financial performance to date.
Consolidated revenues grew 15% to INR 1,136,626 Mn, 
supported by a 17% increase in EBITDA to INR 108,775 
Mn, and a remarkable 40% rise in PAT (concern share) 
to INR 38,030 Mn. Capital efficiency continued to 
improve despite significant investments in new 
Greenfield facilities and acquisitions, with Return on 
Capital Employed (ROCE) rising to 17.2% (17.7% on a 
normalised basis). 
With our booked business now exceeding USD 88 Bn, 
we have clear visibility into upcoming customer 
programmes. These achievements reflect the strength 
of our diversified business model, the resilience of our 
teams, and the continued trust of our customers. As we 
close Vision 2025, we begin a new chapter with Vision 
2030. This letter reflects on the journey so far, the 
discipline that shaped it, and the future we are building 
together with all our stakeholders.
Theme of this year
The theme of this year’s Annual Report is “Great 
achievements come to teams who collectively believe 
in their dreams.” This spirit of belief, discipline, and 
perseverance has guided Motherson throughout its 
50-year journey, especially over the past five years.
As we celebrate this important milestone, I’m reminded 
that our journey has always been shaped by shared 
dreams. From our earliest days, we aspired to be a 
company that could contribute meaningfully to our 
customers, society, and our people. That ambition 
remains unchanged.We reflect more on this journey in 
the dedicated 50-year history 
section of this report. But at the 
heart of it is a simple truth: every 
step forward is built on the trust of 
our customers. From wiring 
harnesses to mirrors, from logistics 
to aerospace and now consumer 
electronics, Motherson has grown 
by responding to our customers’ 
evolving needs and building the 
solutions they require. That principle 
continues to guide us.
Today, Motherson is a global 
organisation with over 425 facilities 
across 44 countries, supporting 
customers across a wide range of 
industries. And yet, our focus 
remains unchanged. We continue 
to deliver high-quality solutions, 
build enduring relationships, and 
create long-term value. 
On behalf of the entire Motherson 
family, I extend my deepest 
gratitude to everyone who has been 
a part of this journey. Thanks to you, 
the reality of what Motherson has 
become has exceeded our wildest 
dreams, and you remain forever in 
our hearts. Your trust and support 
continue to inspire us. As we move 
forward, we do so with confidence 
and humility, still inspired by the 
same shared dreams that first set us 
on this path.
Vision 2025 overview 
In 2020, we launched Vision 2025 
with a bold aspiration: to reach USD 36 billion in revenues with 40% 
ROCE. These were not easy targets. 
But they provided us with direction, 
pushed us beyond our comfort 
zones, and kept us focused during 
one of the most unpredictable five-
year periods in the industry.
What made this period especially 
challenging was the environment in 
which we delivered. The COVID-19 
pandemic brought production to a 
halt, disrupted lives and supply 
chains globally. Even after the 
pandemic, volatility remained high. 
The industry faced semiconductor 
shortages, supply bottlenecks, and 
sharp increases in energy and 
commodity prices. Broader 
inflation, shifting regulations, and 
regional conflicts added further 
uncertainty. In many ways, elevated 
energy costs and global instability 
have become the new normal.
And yet, through all this volatility, we 
remained focused on our purpose 
and delivered one of the strongest 
five-year performances in our 
history. We began this journey with 
revenues of around USD 9 billion. 
Five years later, we closed the  
cycle with USD 25.7 billion in gross 
revenues. We came very close  
to achieving the USD 36 billion 
target in top-line. There were ample 
acquisition opportunities that could 
have taken us beyond it, but they 
did not align with our terms. And 
that matters to us. At Motherson, 
we have always believed that

about creating real value, 
maintaining financial discipline, and 
ensuring that every investment 
supports long-term performance. 
That approach has always helped

was shaped directly by what our

through new technologies and

became a Tier 0.5 supplier, managing complete cockpit 
and door module assemblies. In aerospace, we became 
a Tier 1 supplier, supporting global programmes 
through precision manufacturing and systems 
integration.

At the same time, our teams continued to deliver 
operational excellence. We improved our net leverage 
to 0.9x, the lowest in the past five years. These are 
numbers, yes, but behind each one lies the effort, 
commitment, and belief of our people around the 
world.
Diversification gives us strength
Our 3CX10 diversification strategy has served us very 
well. It has ensured that we are not overly dependent 
on any one customer, country, or component. This 
balance gives us the flexibility to adapt, the resilience  
to face disruptions, and the confidence to plan for the 
long term.
A key part of our diversification is our globally local 
strategy. We aim to produce locally, with local teams, 
for local customers. This enables us to respond faster, 
manage costs more effectively, and build strong local 
teams. We also maintain a balanced global footprint, 
with over 50% of our revenues coming from emerging 
markets, while maintaining a solid presence in 
developed ones. This enables us to benefit from both 
growth and stability, while staying connected to key 
trends across major regions.
We have already achieved our 3CX10 goal on the 
customer front and are making steady progress on the 
component and country fronts. No single customer 
accounts for more than 10% of our revenues. This 
balanced exposure supports stability and helps us  
to focus on building long-term partnerships.
Our product offerings are also largely powertrain 
agnostic. Whether it is ICE, hybrid, or EV platforms,  
this allows us to support OEMs across different 
technologies and transitions without being tied to  
any single drivetrain.
As we move forward, we will continue to diversify our 
offerings and footprint in line with the evolving needs of 
our customers.
Finding new avenues for growth
This year, our non-automotive businesses crossed INR 
3,100 crores in revenue, growing more than 100% from 
the previous year. That tells us we are moving in the In the Health & Medical division, we 
continued to expand our presence 
and capabilities. A new Greenfield 
facility in Chennai and the 
acquisition of Irillic strengthened 
our offerings in surgical imaging 
and high-precision components. In 
the consumer electronics industry, 
right direction. In the aerospace 
division, we now operate 17 facilities 
across India, Europe, and North 
Africa. The acquisition of AD 
Industries brings us deeper 
machining capabilities, helping us 
support critical engine parts with 
precision and consistency. 
9chapter 3 chairman’s letter
annual report  2024-2025our journey has just begun. Our  
first facility is now operational, and 
we have successfully delivered the 
initial batch of products. It’s a proud 
milestone because it marks the start 
of something much bigger. We are 
now building what will become the 
largest Motherson facility in the 
world, and one of the biggest of its 
kind in India. Interestingly, it is for an 
entirely new customer who came to 
us because of our past performance 
and our capability to deliver quickly 
and keep our promises.
Creating value through ROCE
Our early investors taught us the 
importance of focusing on Return 
on Capital Employed (ROCE) to 
measure how efficiently we utilise 
capital and ensure long-term 
profitability. Even in a year with 
heavy investments, including new 
Greenfield facilities and growth-
focused CAPEX, we were able to 
improve our ROCE. This reflects the 
collective effort across our teams, 
constantly optimising, improving, 
and making every investment 
count.
What makes ROCE especially 
powerful is its universality. Everyone 
can contribute to it — whether  
it’s improving machine uptime, 
optimising floor space, or 
streamlining inventory and supply 
chains. Each small action adds  
up, turning day-to-day efforts into 
shared success. It brings the group 
together, from the shop floor to 
strategy, around one clear objective: 
creating more value from every  
unit of capital.In a group as diverse as ours, ROCE 
also gives us a clear lens to evaluate 
performance across our businesses. 
With our net leverage ratio 
improving to 0.9x, we have the 
strength and flexibility to continue 
investing in the future while staying 
true to our financial discipline. 
Vision 2030 — a new chapter 
begins
In 1995, we set our first 5-year plan 
and have done so every 5 years 
since then, at the suggestion of our 
investors. Every plan has given us 
direction and has been much more 
than just a set of numbers. They 
have challenged us to venture far 
outside our comfort zones, thereby 
enabling us to grow both as 
individuals and as a company.
As we conclude Vision 2025, we 
turn our sights to the future with 
Vision 2030. The specific targets of 
Vision 2030 have been shared on 
page 50. The direction is already 
clear. We will:
• Grow content per vehicle
• Continue to explore new industries
•  Strengthen our position in 
emerging markets
•  Invest in sustainability, talent, and 
technologyVision 2030 is more than a business ambition. It is a 
reflection of the future we aspire to build. It’s not just 
about reaching our goals but about staying true to  
how and why we pursue them. Guided by our values, 
rooted in long-term thinking, and driven by a deep 
sense of purpose, Vision 2030 reflects our responsibility 
to create lasting value for our people, customers, 
investors, and the world around us.
 
Looking ahead, with gratitude
Fifty years ago, we started with INR 1,000 and a dream. 
We didn’t know where life would take us, but we knew 
how we wanted to walk through it, with humility, 
discipline, and purpose.
Today, we look back with gratitude. To our customers, 
thank you for trusting us to be part of your journey. To 
our employees, who have stood with us, grown with  
us, and made every milestone possible. To our 
investors, thank you for your continued support and 
guidance through all the ups and downs. To our 
partners, for sharing their knowledge and helping us 
deliver the best solutions to our customers. And to the 
authorities, banks, and institutions that have supported 
us over the years. Vision 2030 is now in front of us and 
it is marking the start of a new chapter. Whether we 
achieve all our dreams is up to the universe. But we will 
give it everything we have.
Thank you for walking this path with us. We hope you 
will be with us on the incredibly exciting journey ahead.
Sincerely,
Vivek Chaand Sehgal

samvardhana motherson international limited 10chapter 4 Q&A with laksh vaaman sehgal
Fifty years of trust.
We had a conversation with Laksh Vaaman Sehgal, Director, SAMIL, 
to better understand the key factors contributing to the good health 
of the business and how the new acquisitions and upcoming plants 
will help drive future growth for Motherson.
Q1 
Motherson completed 50 years in FY25 — a 
remarkable milestone in its journey. What does 
this moment represent for the Group, and how 
is it shaping the way forward as we prepare for 
the next phase of growth?
When my grandmother and father started the 
Motherson journey, no one in their wildest imagination 
would have thought we would make such great strides 
and build a global business that has lasted 50 years 
while at the same time sowing the seeds for future 
growth. It is a testament to the philosophy and business 
ethics ingrained into our ecosystem to do more and the 
endless virtuous loop of “Return on Trust”.
We have evolved from a single-component, single-
customer business to a global design, engineering, 
manufacturing and assembly powerhouse supporting 
customers across a wide range of industries. In the last 
5 years we created a strong platform for growth called 
Motherson 2.0 where we not only recognised the 
business but also proactively took steps to be geared 
for the next leg of growth by focusing on creating 
industry agnostic capabilities. 
With over ~3,000 patents as of March 31, 2025 we have 
now evolved into a technology and design partner to 
support the entire product lifecycle. A testament to our 
capabilities is the entry into new segments such as 
consumer electronics at the behest of the customer as 
well as making inroads to support the value chain for 
semiconductor industry.
Our approach to sustainable business growth remains 
the same; reactive to the changing business 
environment and opportunities that volatility throws up, 
addressing the pain points in the supply chain. All of this is done with a robust evaluation 
framework and financial prudence. 
As we turn the page to the next 
five-year plan, Vision 2030, we are 
entering a new phase of growth 
where in we continue to evolve with 
the changing times. We coin this as  
Motherson 3.0 as we leverage the 
strong foundation and well-
diversified business model to build 
and incubate new businesses 
based on our three pillars of growth.
Q2 
How would you assess 
Motherson’s performance 
against the strategic 
objectives set out in Vision 
2025?
Vision 2025 gave us a bold and 
ambitious direction to position 
Motherson as a globally respected, 
customer-centric solutions provider, 
with the target of reaching $36 
billion in revenues, with 25% from 
non-automotive segments and 75% 
from automotive. This vision 
challenged us to think bigger, scale 
faster, and build a more diversified 
and resilient organisation. 
It is notable to mention that during 
this period the global automotive 
industry also went through a down 
cycle with production growing at CAGR of 1.4%. The production levels 
in developed markets still have not 
caught up to pre-COVID levels as a 
result of which there is excess 
capacity. Over the past five years, 
our gross revenues grew from $9.6 
billion to $25.7 billion (at constant 
currency) registering a growth of 2.7 
times during this five year period.
We completed 23 strategic 
acquisitions and 5 strategic 
partnerships broadening our 
technological capabilities, customer 
base, and global footprint. All of 
these strategic acquisitions support 
our diversification journey, whether 
through forging stronger 
relationships with customers 
(existing and new), enhancing 
technological capabilities and 
product portfolios, or expanding 
our geographic presence. For 
instance, with the acquisition of 
SAS we were able to cement our 
position as a Tier-0.5 supplier with 
just-in-time & just-in-sequence 
assembly lines to support 
customers. This asset enabled us to 
establish a new division of 
Integrated Assemblies and is now 
able to realise greater group 
synergies in the form of bundling of 
RFQs, insourcing new programs 
enabling Motherson to be a single 
window solutions provider. We are

now working towards enhancing 
the product portfolio from cockpit

establishing complete vehicle

Diversification and de-risking have 
been core to our strategy. We have 
made strong inroads into high-
potential non-automotive sectors 
such as aerospace, health and 
medical, logistics, and consumer 
electronics. Whether as the fastest-
growing aerospace supplier or 
through the construction of our 
largest-ever factory for consumer 
electronics, our newer verticals are 
scaling with speed and confidence.
The most important metric for us is 
Return on Capital Employed, which 
is diligently monitored across all 
operational units and business 
divisions. For FY2025 SAMIL 
delivered a ROCE of 17.2%, despite 
the capex for greenfield expansions 
and M&A payouts. This reflects 
disciplined execution and a long-

value.
Vision 2025 has enabled Motherson 
to become a more capable, 
confident, and future-ready 
organisation. It has laid the 
foundation for our next phase of 
growth that is Vision 2030, as we 
continue building a stronger, more 
diversified Motherson that serves 
customers across industries with 
excellence and integrity.Q3
Can you talk about the key 
acquisitions and partnerships 
and what value they bring to 
the Group? 
We continued to strengthen our 
capabilities through strategic 
acquisitions and partnerships. We 
have a robust M&A evaluation 
framework with a strike rate of less 
than 5% on the opportunities that 
we evaluate. Each acquisition is at 
the behest of the customers to 
ensure sustainable long-term 
growth within the Motherson 
ecosystem. Since the start of fiscal 
2024-25, we successfully closed 
and integrated 6 acquisitions. A 
good example of this at play is the 
recent Atsumi acquisition. The 
asset, with its world-class 
machining capabilities and high-
value-add processes such as heat 
treatment, carburising, grinding, 
and broaching housed in-house, 
has a well-balanced footprint across 
both emerging and developed 
markets. However, it was largely 
exposed to one single customer, 
primarily for ICE components. 
Under the Motherson umbrella, we 
are not only leveraging group 
synergies through the 
complementary capabilities in India 
and Mexico but are also fast-
tracking our pivot to new industries 
by addressing the backward 
integration requirements of 
Consumer Electronics as well as 
opening new avenues for 
Aerospace.
We also entered into multiple new 
strategic partnerships with 
technology leaders namely; BIEL 
Crystal, Matsui, Sanko, Hamakyorex, 
and Egtronics to provide a whole "Localisation and 
integration help us 
support customers 
efficiently across 
industries, 
strengthening trust 
globally."
Pankaj Mital 
Whole-time Director & Chief Operating Officer

customers across industries. These

Q4
Despite the market 
conditions, Motherson 
announced a number of new 
Greenfield facilities in FY25. 
Could you share some light on 
the thought process behind 
incurring large capital 
expenditures?
Our organic expansion continues to 
be customer-driven, with new 
facilities established on the back of 
firm commitments. Despite ongoing 
volatility in market dynamics and a 
challenging production environment, 
we successfully operationalised  
10 new facilities across multiple 
businesses and geographies during 
the year. An additional 14 facilities  are currently under various stages  
of development, with rollout 
progressing in alignment with 
customer readiness and local 
execution timelines.
It is a known fact that automotive 
production in many developed 
markets remains 10–15% below pre-
pandemic levels, resulting in spare 
capacity across the industry. This 
makes our diversified and resilient 
business model even more critical. 
All of our new facilities are being  
set up in high-growth, emerging 
markets, such as India, Poland, the 
UAE, China, and Mexico, thereby 
supporting a broad spectrum of 
businesses.
Notable among these is our 
significant investment in the 
consumer electronics segment with 
three new facilities. One of these 
will be the largest in Motherson’s 
global ecosystem and, upon 
completion, the largest single-block 
industrial building in India. Another 
key initiative involves leveraging our 
aerospace capabilities to support 
customers in manufacturing  
high-precision components used  
in semiconductor fabrication

Q5
The passenger vehicle segment in Europe and 
North America has witnessed some softness. 
How is this affecting Motherson and how are 
we mitigating these challenges? 
We are a well-diversified player, whether in terms of the 
regions we operate in, the products we produce, or the 
customers we supply. There will always be some 
regional challenges but when you look at it at a global 
level things get balanced as some regions would do 
better than others. 
Developed markets like Europe and the US are still 
below pre-COVID levels in terms of production volumes 
of light vehicles, while emerging markets like India and 
China have surpassed their pre-COVID volumes. Our 
portfolio generates equal revenue from developed and 
emerging markets and hence the impact of regional 
volatilities gets muted. 
While softness in developed markets creates 
opportunities for us to solve supply chain issues at the 
behest of our customers. Having completed over 23 
acquisitions and having made significant investments 
globally, we also need to adapt and recalibrate our 
operations to breathe with the market, for which we 
have proactively initiated a series of transformative 
measures in Central and Western Europe. In order to 
maintain competitiveness in the region we will be 
addressing optimisation of cost block of approximately 
EUR 50 million per annum. Once fully executed the 
growth in Emerging markets provides rapid scale up 
opportunities. As a matter of fact, we are expanding our 
presence in higher-growth areas like India, Mexico, and 
parts of Asia. Our non-automotive businesses are also 
gaining traction.  
So while w e are seeing short-term pressure in some 
pockets, our overall platform remains well balanced. 
That thinking continues to guide how we operate and 
how we grow.
15chapter 4 Q&A with laksh vaaman sehgal
annual report  2024-2025Q6
How is the company 
positioning itself to leverage 
the growing presence of 
Chinese auto manufacturers 
both domestically and 
globally?
Chinese OEMs are becoming more 
important in the global automotive 
landscape. They are expanding 
rapidly into new markets, with a 
strong focus on electrification and 
software-defined vehicles. This shift 
is creating new opportunities for us, 
both within China and in other 
regions where these customers are 
growing.
We already have a strong 
manufacturing presence in China. 
Over the years, we have built 
trusted relationships with many of 
the leading Chinese OEMs and 
Tier-1s. Our teams in China are well 
aligned with their expectations 
regarding cost, speed, and quality. 
That base is helping us expand with 
them as they enter other markets.
We are also seeing increased 
interest from Chinese OEMs in 
localising in Europe, Mexico, and 
parts of Southeast Asia. As we 
already operate in these regions, we 
are well-positioned to support them 
with local manufacturing and 
engineering.
As Chinese OEMs expand globally, 
we are committed to being a 
reliable and responsible partner to 
them on that journey.Q7
In light of ongoing global tariff 
tensions and protectionist 
policies, what impact do you 
foresee for Motherson, and 
how are we positioning 
ourselves to remain resilient?
The global business environment is 
becoming increasingly complex 
and uncertain, shaped by shifting 
regulatory landscapes, evolving 
trade dynamics, and a renewed 
emphasis on onshoring in several 
economies. Recent developments 
around tariffs, reciprocal trade 
measures, application of duties and 
new trade agreements have 
disrupted the global automotive 
supply chain and introduced new 
layers of unpredictability. 
In this context, Motherson’s long-
standing globally local strategy 
continues to serve us well. We have 
always believed in a decentralised, 
customer-centric approach; one 
that prioritises proximity and speed 
of response. Today, we operate in 
44 countries, with local teams, 
manufacturing facilities, and 
supplier ecosystems. This structure 
significantly reduces risk and 
enhances our ability to adapt to 
region-specific challenges.
For instance, a significant portion of 
our U.S. sales is USMCA-compliant. 
For the remaining share, we are 
proactively engaging with our customers to identify pragmatic solutions; whether 
through alternative sourcing or the structured pass-
through of tariff-related direct costs. 
While there may be some near-term pain as customers 
recalibrate their supply chains to these new realities, we 
remain a dependable, sustainable solutions provider 
across cycles and geographies.
This is one of the reasons we continue to invest in 
localisation and vertical integration. It gives us better 
control over cost, delivery, and compliance, regardless 
of where the product is manufactured or where it is to 
be shipped. That mindset will continue to guide us as 
the global situation evolves.

strategic partnership with BIEL Crystal, marking a 
significant step in expanding our presence into this new 
segment.
Our journey so far is progressing well, both in terms of 
capability-building and customer engagement. The first 
facility became operational in the second half of FY25 
and saw a sharp ramp-up in production. Two more 
Greenfield facilities are on track, with SOPs expected in

that’s how we grow together.

Q9
Can you highlight the progress and growth 
observed across Motherson’s new business 
divisions over the past year?
Our diversification into new businesses continues to be 
a thoughtfully guided and exciting journey. During this 
strategic vision period, we incubated and scaled four 
key verticals: Aerospace, Health & Medical, Logistics, 
and Technology & Industrial Solutions. Our approach 
has been grounded in a clear philosophy—first, to 
understand pain points across the value chain, then 
identify how we could address them, whether through 
our existing capabilities or by forming strategic 
partnerships and acquisitions. This has allowed us to 
establish strong foundational platforms with a long-
term view toward consolidation and scale.
The Aerospace division is a prime example of this 
strategy in action. What began organically has since 
been strengthened by the acquisitions of CIM Tools and 
AD Industries. Today, the division operates across 17 
facilities in four countries; India, France, Morocco, and 
Tunisia offering a healthy balance of near-shore and 
best-cost locations. We have built a comprehensive 
suite of capabilities in advanced metal fabrication, 
machining, composites, and surface treatment. These 
capabilities have been developed in a phased manner 
and are deployed horizontally across the aerospace 
value chain to maximise impact and scalability.With a sizeable booked business of 
USD 1.3 billion to be realised over 
the next 5 years, the division has 
built a strong base. Our consistent 
efforts have been recognised by 
Airbus, which recently empanelled 
us as a Tier-1 supplier across their 
entire product portfolio, including 
commercial, helicopter, and 
advanced systems. This milestone 
provides us with meaningful access 
to large RFQ programmes rather 
than small packages. 
Our capabilities have also opened 
doors to adjacent opportunities. We 
are now establishing a new facility 
to supply components for 
specialised equipment used in 
manufacturing semiconductors, 
further diversifying our customer 
base.Similarly, our Logistics business 
continues to scale meaningfully. We 
have deepened our collaboration 
with existing partner Hamakyorex 
and formed a new strategic alliance 
with Sanko. These partnerships are 
aimed at delivering end-to-end 
logistics solutions that not only 
optimise our internal supply chain 
spend but also serve external 
customers with greater efficiency 
and value.
These businesses are being built 
with care, with customer 
involvement from the start, and with 
a focus on creating long-term value.
17chapter 4 Q&A with laksh vaaman sehgal
annual report  2024-2025Q10  
Could you share some of the 
major sustainability initiatives 
and achievements for the 
Group in FY25?
Sustainability is no longer a 
separate topic at Motherson. It is 
part of how we work, make 
decisions, and grow responsibly. 
FY25 marked the close of our Vision 
2025 plan and gave us a moment to 
reflect on how far we have come. 
Today, we are present in 44 
countries, and with this growth 
comes a greater responsibility—to 
our people, customers, 
communities, and the planet.
Our climate transition strategy 
continues to guide our actions. We 
remain committed to achieving net 
zero for Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 2040 and Scope 3 carbon neutrality 
by 2050. This year, over 100 sites 
were certified for ISO 50001, and 
we expanded our use of 
renewables, process efficiency, and 
real-time energy monitoring. On 
Scope 3, we increased supplier 
engagement and deepened 
collaboration on sustainable 
packaging and logistics, including a 
joint venture with Sanko Japan. As 
we advance on our sustainability 
journey, a closer analysis of our 
internal data has helped us identify 
opportunities to improve efficiency 
and reduce our carbon footprint. 
One key initiative in this direction 
has been the establishment of 
energy division focused on 
generating and sourcing renewable 
energy, be it solar, wind, or hydro for 
captive consumption, thereby 
reducing our reliance on grid 
electricity. Several projects are 
currently at various stages of 
implementation, with the long-term 
goal of scaling these efforts across 
our global operations.
We also strengthened our work in 
water conservation, circularity, and 
biodiversity. More than half of our 
plants are in water-stressed regions, 
and we’ve taken practical steps to 
reduce water use, improve reuse, 
and promote rainwater harvesting. 
In biodiversity, we now use IBAT 
(Integrated Biodiversity Assessment 
Tool) across our footprint to assess 
risks and restoration needs, with 
local teams leading tree planting 
and conservation actions.
Social and governance topics 
remained a strong focus. We 
expanded the Mental Health First 
Aiders programme, strengthened leadership development, and launched new inclusion 
initiatives. At the same time, we completed over 440 
community projects across regions. These efforts 
remind us that sustainability is about more than just 
targets—it’s about earning the trust of our stakeholders 
and being ready to take on greater responsibility for the 
future.
Q11 
As we look ahead to Vision 2030, how is 
Motherson evolving its overall strategic 
approach to achieve its long-term objectives 
and deepen its value creation across industries 
and geographies?
As we step into Vision 2030, we do so from a position 
of strength, built on the robust platform during Vision 
2025. Motherson is no longer just an automotive 
components company, we have evolved into a global 
powerhouse in design, engineering, manufacturing, 
and assembly. Our proven track record and deep 
customer trust have enabled us to successfully diversify 
into new sectors, including aerospace and consumer 
electronics, the latter of which welcomed us with a 
significant order based solely on our capabilities and 
credibility. 
This journey of transformation is powered by our 
unique “entrepreneurship within the group” philosophy, 
where each acquisition and business retains its identity, 
autonomy and management while benefiting from 
Motherson’s central functions such as purchasing, 
financial excellence, M&A, IT, and sustainability. 
This dual model fosters innovation, drives integration 
synergies, and accelerates capability building. 
Customer-led diversification remains a core strength, 
one that not only addresses complex supply chain 
challenges but also creates long-term, sustainable 
partnerships. From establishing a strong local base to 
scaling through strategic bolt-ons, we have consistently 
demonstrated our ability to expand with purpose and 
precision. With bold ambitions and robust 
fundamentals, Motherson is poised for an exciting new 
phase of growth under Vision 2030.

What began as a simple partnership between

organisation of over 200,000 people. Over

our partners, our people—and everyone who has been part of 
Motherson over the years. Their trust and commitment have 
shaped every step we have taken.

actions we took to serve better, grow responsibly, and build for 
the long term.

53 annual report  2024-2025chapter 11 vision 2030
Vision 
2030 .
When we told our investors around the year
2000, that we had successfully completed
our 5-year plan targets that we had set in
1995, they made an important remark, “If you
are so convinced about your ability to achieve
such targets, you should publish them in your
annual report.” And that is what we have done
ever since.
Vision 2030 is our 7th 5-year plan. Our targets
have always been ambitious. In fact, when we
set those goals, they were always “seemingly
impossible”. And yet, we have in many cases
achieved or exceeded them, or come close
to achieving them.
Some people tell us we should set goals
that we know we can achieve. But at
Motherson, we believe it is good to stretch
ourselves and not be sure if we will achieve
them or not. That way, ambitious targets pull
us out of our comfort zone. That is where
the real growth happens. Our 5-year plans
help us discover what we are truly capable of.
In the end, however, our targets are about
more than the numbers. It is not just about
where we will end up five years from now.
The true reward is who we become along
the way. 
As a company and as individuals, we start this 
five-year plan, we do not know exactly where 
we will reach and who we will be in 2030. But 
we do know that no day will be boring. Every 
day will bring a new challenge, a new 
opportunity. And we will give everything we 
have, each step of the way. We hope you will 
join us on this journey.

Global economic outlook – 2025:  
Stability amid complexity
According to the IMF’s World Economic Outlook (April 
2025), global GDP growth is projected to moderate to 
2.8% in 2025, down from the earlier estimate of 3.3%1 
and significantly below the pre-pandemic average  
of 3.7% (2000–2019). The global economy having 
seasoned through years of unprecedented disruptions 
started to show resilience and signs of stabilisation in 
2024, however, this is now being tested by significant 
shift in the global policies and framework with the 
following factors; 
•  Evolving trade dynamics and high tariff levels across 
geographies
•  Heightened geopolitical tension and conflict across 
Ukraine-Russia, the Middle East etc.•  Interest rates remained high with 
rate cuts now coming into effect 
•  Core inflation remains at elevated 
levels reflecting service driven 
pressures 
There are some upsides with 
cooling of trade tensions and 
ongoing negotiations on new trade 
agreements to further curb 
uncertainty and limit trade 
disruptions and improve  
consumer confidence. 
Growth in the US is expected to be 
slow due to evolving trade 
dynamics and tariff related front-loading and uncertainty 
around changing policies. Despite 
these headwinds the market 
remains resilient. The Eurozone is 
experiencing slow but stable 
growth with the ongoing trade and 
policy ambiguity. Germany, the 
largest economy remains 
particularly exposed coupled with 
elevated energy costs is now 
pivoting from fiscal restraint to 
expansionary policy. 
The global economy stands at a 
critical inflection point, with 
policymakers navigating the dual 
challenge of maintaining domestic 
stability while strengthening 
multilateral cooperation. Central 
banks across major economies 
continue to calibrate monetary 
policy in response to persistent  
core inflation, driven by structural 
pressures in services and labour 
markets, despite easing headline 
inflation. Therefore, policymakers 
are proceeding cautiously toward 
potential easing to mitigate 
downside risks, build resilience,  
and address long-standing global 
imbalances.

2025: Enduring momentum 
and growing confidence
India continues to stand out as one 
of the world’s most dynamic and 
resilient economies in 2025. 
According to the IMF, India is 
projected to grow at 6.2%1 through 
2025, while estimates from the 
Reserve Bank of India remain GDP forecast by region in percentage

samvardhana motherson international limitedMacroeconomic factors and industry

Our financial performance continues to be closely tied 
to the sales of automotive components supplied to 
global OEM customers across diverse sectors such as 
passenger and commercial vehicles, rail transport, off-
highway machinery, and agricultural equipment. Our 
production levels are inherently linked to the vehicle 
production volumes of our OEM clients, and, as such, 
our operational and financial outcomes are influenced 
by broader economic and industry-specific factors.
Key macroeconomic drivers such as interest rate Business environment.
trends, commodity price 
movements, geopolitical risks,  
and cost fluctuations in materials 
and labour continue to shape the 
operating landscape. These factors 
not only impact our input costs and 
working capital requirements, but 
also the demand environment - 
especially in price-sensitive end 
markets where vehicle affordability 
plays a crucial role in influencing 
buying decisions.

=== page 33 ===
Evolving input-cost landscape
Following a brief period of stability in FY2023-24, 
FY2024-25 saw a renewed surge in global commodity 
prices—most notably for copper and aluminium – 
driven by a combination of supply constraints, 
accelerated infrastructure spending across multiple 
economies, and stronger-than-anticipated industrial 
demand, particularly from China and Southeast Asia. 
Copper prices, in particular, have seen a significant 
uptick due to increased usage in electric vehicles (EVs), 
renewable energy, and grid expansion projects.
Aluminium, another key input for our product portfolio, 
is also witnessing price volatility due to disruptions in 
global mining and refining operations, as well as 
ongoing demand from sectors focused on light-
weighting and sustainability. In response, we are 
actively working with our customers to implement cost 
pass-through mechanisms and improve our 
procurement strategies. We are also exploring supply 
chain diversification and product-level engineering 
optimisation to mitigate the impact of cost pressures.
Energy prices and sustainability transition 
Energy markets have entered a phase of structural 
transition rather than temporary volatility. While the 
sharp spikes seen in 2022 have moderated, energy 
prices remain elevated, especially in regions like Europe 
where natural gas and electricity markets are still 
adjusting to shifts away from Russian supply. This has 
prompted a broader industry-wide focus on energy 
efficiency, contract restructuring, and power purchase 
agreements with renewable sources. Our facilities 
continue to invest in energy-saving initiatives—ranging 
from advanced process control systems to renewable 
energy sourcing—aimed at reducing both operational 
costs and carbon footprint. These efforts are 
increasingly aligned with the decarbonisation goals of 
our customers and are becoming integral to long-term 
competitiveness and ESG performance.
Inflation and interest rates across key regions
In FY25, inflation remained relatively stable across key 
economies. The European Union recorded inflation at 
2.3% in Q4 FY2024-25, slightly down from 2.6% in Q4 
FY2023-24. The United States also saw a moderate 
decline – from 3.3% to 2.7% – while India experienced a more significant drop in inflation, 
from 5.0% to 3.7%, reflecting 
improved supply conditions and 
monetary discipline. 
Interest rate trends diverged across 
regions. In India, rates remained 
relatively stable moving from 6.5% 
in Q4 FY2023-24 to 6.3% in Q4 
FY2024-25, reinforcing the Reserve 
Bank’s focus on inflation anchoring 
and currency management. The 
U.S. eased rates from 5.4% to 4.5%, 
potentially to balance growth 
concerns. Meanwhile, the European 
Union moved more decisively, 
reducing rates from 4.5% to 2.7%, 
indicating a shift toward monetary 
easing in the face of slowing 
demand. For the automotive industry,  
this environment offers both 
opportunities and constraints. In 
India, falling inflation supports cost 
stability and consumer confidence, 
but high borrowing costs could 
restrain retail financing – particularly 
for price-sensitive segments like 
two-wheelers and entry-level 
passenger vehicles. In the EU, lower 
interest rates may stimulate vehicle 
purchases, though the subdued 
inflation points to broader demand-
side softness. Overall, while 
inflationary pressures have abated, 
high or diverging interest rate 
regimes remain a critical factor 
influencing investment decisions, 
financing strategies, and consumer 
behaviour across global automotive 
markets.

Supply chain resilience and 
logistics volatility
Global supply chains continued to 
stabilise through 2024, with notable 
improvements in material 
availability, logistics lead times, and 
production alignment across the 
automotive sector. However, new 
forms of fragility have emerged. 
Maritime insecurity in the Red Sea, 
regional conflicts, and volatile fuel 
costs led to a sharp but temporary 
spike in freight rates early in 
FY2024-25 – nearly doubling from 
late FY2023-24 levels, reaching 
around USD 6,000 per 40-foot 
container. These rates subsequently 
declined and remained relatively 
stable before easing further toward 
the end of the period. Despite these 
pressures, the industry has shown remarkable resilience. Supply chain 
strategies have matured 
significantly, with companies 
adopting dual-sourcing, regional 
supplier networks, and predictive 
planning tools. In our own 
operations, we have strengthened 
supplier diversification, optimised 
inventory buffers, and deployed 
multi-modal transport solutions to 
ensure delivery reliability and 
continuity of supply. 
Normalisation of 
semiconductor supply
The acute global semiconductor 
shortage that once severely 
constrained vehicle production has 
largely normalised during FY2024-
25. Foundry capacity expansions, 
diversified sourcing strategies, and 
improved inventory management 
across OEMs and Tier-1 suppliers 
have led to more predictable 
supply. While some mismatch 
between demand and availability 
remains—particularly for advanced 
chips used in premium models and 
EVs—the broader impact on our 
operations has significantly 
reduced. We continue to maintain 
close coordination with key 
suppliers to ensure visibility and 
responsiveness across our value 
chain, particularly as the electronic 
content in vehicles continues to 
rise.
Climate policy and regulatory 
shifts
A notable emerging theme is the 
growing influence of climate-related 
policies and sustainability 
regulations on the automotive 
sector. Several regions have 
introduced stricter emissions 
norms, localisation mandates, and 
green manufacturing incentives, affecting everything 
from production processes to product design. For 
component manufacturers like us, this means adjusting 
to evolving customer requirements for lighter, more 
efficient, and recyclable parts, while also aligning with 
mandatory ESG disclosures and compliance standards 
across markets. This trend is reshaping procurement 
strategies, capital allocation, and long-term planning, 
and is likely to become an even more defining aspect of 
the business environment over the next few years. 
Labour and talent pressures
Labour markets remain tight in several key regions, 
including North America and Europe, where skilled 
workforce availability and wage inflation continue to 
pose challenges. Additionally, rising expectations 
around workplace safety, automation integration, and 
flexible employment models are reshaping workforce 
strategies. We are responding through targeted hiring, 
skill development programmes, and the gradual 
introduction of automation in areas prone to labour 
shortages or inefficiencies.
Conclusion
As we move through 2025, the broader business 
environment continues to be shaped by a delicate 
balance of economic normalisation and structural 
transformation. Geopolitical tensions and elevated 
input costs remain key risks, but improved supply chain 
agility, digitisation, and increased operational resilience 
across the industry are helping companies adapt. We 
remain focused on disciplined cost management, 
proactive customer engagement, and operational 
agility to navigate this evolving landscape.

We stay resilient by 
adapting to change  
and staying aligned  
with customer needs.

regions. The global automotive production remained 
muted at an aggregate level as a result of growth 
varied across key geographies led by China

Despite near-term softness, the automotive industry 
continues to undergo fundamental transformation. 
Electrification, localisation of supply chains, and 
digitalisation of vehicle platforms are reshaping 
production strategies globally. While developed 
markets recalibrate post-pandemic demand and 
policy responses, emerging economies in Asia 
particularly India and China are increasingly becoming 
the engines of growth, investment, and innovation.
Global light vehicle development  
Fiscal year 2025 turned out to be an exceptionally 
challenging period for the global automotive industry, 
marked by continued structural transformation and 
macroeconomic volatility. OEMs were forced to 
reassess and recalibrate their strategies on model 
launches and powertrain configurations. This was 
driven in part by divergent electric vehicle (EV) 
adoption rates across geographies, prompting a  
more cautious and region-specific approach to 
portfolio planning.
Consumer sentiment remained subdued, with buyers 
becoming increasingly mindful of discretionary 
spending, especially in the face of weak economic 
growth, inflationary pressures, and economic 
uncertainty in key markets. This cautious demand 
environment added further complexity to OEMs’ 
planning and production cycles.
The global auto industry 
continues to evolve, and 
we remain aligned to the 
needs of our customers.
65 annual report  2024-2025chapter 13  global automotive industry
Compounding these challenges 
was the evolving landscape of 
global trade dynamics. 
Uncertainties surrounding tariff 
regimes and cross-border duties 
continued to impact sourcing 
strategies and cost structures. The 
effects of these tariffs are difficult to 
isolate in any single region, resulting 
in operational disruptions such as 
supply chain dislocations, inventory 
imbalances, and unpredictable 
shifts in vehicle program timelines 
as OEMs continue to adjust their 
future production plans.
Despite these headwinds, the 
industry grew at a modest CAGR of 
approximately 3.8% between FY2020-21 and FY2024-25. This 
growth trajectory reflects a recovery 
from the pandemic lows, but was 
tempered by prolonged supply 
chain disruptions and 
semiconductor shortages that 
persisted well into FY2022-23. As 
the industry continues to evolve, 
OEMs and suppliers alike are 
recognising the need to build more 
agile, resilient, and technology-
driven operating models to adapt to 
the uncertainties of a fast-changing 
mobility landscape.
Global commercial vehicle 
production development 
The global commercial vehicle 
production for the fiscal year 2024-25 was 3.3 million units, a decline of 8.9% 
compared to the previous fiscal year. While over the 
medium term, the industry is expected to grow, fiscal 
year 2024-25 volumes were negatively impacted by 
macroeconomic weakness in some regions affecting 
freight and construction activity. The announcement  
of trade restrictions by the new U.S. administrations 
further clouded industry prospects as it introduced 
uncertainty regarding future direction of the global 
economy and complicated operational planning of 
customers. While the major regions saw production 
volumes decline, Europe saw the largest drop of 23.9% 
after the introduction of new regulations resulted in 
significant prebuying in the previous fiscal year. While 
facing near term uncertainty, OEMs are also adjusting 
to industry trends such as stricter emission standards, 
digitalisation and increased automation capabilities of 
commercial vehicles.

66chapter 13 global automotive industry
samvardhana motherson international limitedLight vehicle and commercial vehicle
Commentary by region  
The following is a brief description of light and
commercial vehicle production in key regions
in which we operate.
Europe
LV production:
Light Vehicle production for the fiscal year 2024-25 was 
16.9 million units. Europe posted the sharpest 
contraction among major regions in FY2024–25. Light 
vehicle production fell by 5.9% compared to FY2023–
24. These figures reflect a combination of softened 
demand, recalibration of EV strategy by major OEMs 
during the year, compared with the strong demand 
environment seen in the previous fiscal year. The pace 
of recovery remains muted given the backdrop of geo-
political tensions and uncertainty around tariff related 
policies.
Commercial production:
Commercial vehicle production declined to 538K units 
in fiscal year 2025 from 706k units in the corresponding 
previous fiscal year, registering a striking degrowth of 
approximately 23.9% as demand was boosted by pre-
buying effects before the General Safety Regulations 
mandate and new Eurovignette rules were coming into 
effect as of July 2024, resulting in a production drop in 
the second half of 2024. Additionally, European trucks 
sales were further negatively impacted by the slow 
infrastructure activity and subdued manufacturing 
environment impacting fleet expansion.
North America
LV production:
North American light vehicle production for the fiscal 
year 2024-25 decreased to15.2 million units from 15.8 
million in the previous fiscal year. The drop in overall 
production of 3.3% is primarily attributed to structural 
issues faced by key OEMs with temporary labour strikes 
during peak production months, inventory adjustments 
and the recently announced policy around tariffs and 
localisation mandates. During the tail end of the year 
there was a pull up of production on account of pre-
buying and inventory build-ups.
Location: Spain
Product: Bumper
Process: Assembly
67 annual report  2024-2025chapter 13  global automotive industry
Commercial production:
Commercial vehicle production for 
the fiscal year 2024-25 was 628K 
units as compared to 683K units in 
the previous fiscal year with an 
output decline of 8.1%. Driven by 
softened freight demand specially 
in the heavy-duty segment resulting 
in deferred fleet investments. This 
was further impacted by production 
volatility contributed by supply 
chain adjustments on account of 
shifting trade and tariff policies.
India
LV production:
In contrast, India emerged as a 
relative bright spot in fiscal year 2024–25. Light vehicle production 
increased from 5.6 million units in 
fiscal year 2023-24 to 5.7 million 
units in fiscal year 2024-25. 
Registering a growth of 1.6% this 
positive uptick is underpinned by 
strong domestic demand 
particularly for compact SUVs along 
with sustained export momentum. 
This is further driven by a stable 
supply chain environment with 
major OEMs also expanding 
capacities for domestic and export 
related production.
Commercial production:
Commercial Vehicle production for 
the fiscal year 2024-25 was 450K units as compared to 487 in the fiscal year 2023-24, 
registering a 7.5% degrowth. This contraction is to be 
viewed as a more normalised volume as the industry 
faced a high base effect from the previous year’s strong 
recovery as a result of which fleet operators are also 
moderating replacement cycles.
China
LV production:
China led the global market in terms of light vehicle 
growth in fiscal year 2024–25 with the production base 
expanding from 29.4 million units in fiscal year 2023-24 
to 30.8 million units, registering a solid 4.8% increase 
year-on-year. This growth was driven by strong 
momentum in new energy vehicles (NEVs) and 
domestic demand recovery supported by government 
incentives. Further Chinese OEMs continued to 
accelerate export expansion to various geographies. 
China’s integrated supply chain and focus on 
electrification positions the region as a key growth 
engine for the global automotive industry in this fiscal 
year.
Commercial production:
Commercial vehicle production in China for the fiscal 
year 2024-25 was 1,125K units as compared to 1,205K 
units for the previous fiscal year, volumes slipped by 
6.6%, driven by a relatively weak domestic economic 
activity and weaker export demand. Stronger demand 
in the second half of fiscal year 2024-25, an extension 
of the commercial vehicle trade-in subsidy program 
and solid economic prospects are expected to support 
commercial vehicle production despite remaining risks 
from trade tariffs.
As markets shift and 
volumes fluctuate, we stay 
close to our customers and 
adapt to their evolving 
production needs.

68chapter 13 global automotive industry
samvardhana motherson international limitedAutomotive mega trends
Increased production in emerging markets
The automotive industry is witnessing a notable shift 
towards emerging markets such as India, Mexico, 
China, Poland, Hungary etc. The trend is driven by the 
need for cost efficiency, supply chain diversification and 
growing demand in respective countries. Automakers 
are increasingly investing in local manufacturing amid 
the evolving market dynamics and shifting regulatory 
policies. Emerging markets in Asia and South America 
account for approximately 48% of fiscal year 2024-25 
global production, expected to increase to 
approximately 50% by fiscal year 2029-30. 
Motherson with its diversification strategy has a 
balanced exposure to developed and emerging 
markets to provide solutions to customers.Evolving supply chain with 
reshoring of packages and 
importance of Tier-0.5 players
The role of tier-1 suppliers is 
evolving as OEMs require greater 
integration of the supply chain, 
agility and innovation. As a result, 
there is an increased inter-
dependency of OEMs on Tier-1 
suppliers which has resulted in a 
high level of collaboration between 
OEMs and suppliers. Suppliers are 
moving beyond the role of only 
providing parts i.e., becoming 
strategic partners in the design and 
innovation process, enabling automotive OEMs to focus on  
the development of platforms, 
whilst suppliers can benefit from 
economies of scale by serving 
customers on a global scale. This 
trend is particularly evident for 
electric vehicle OEMs, as such 
manufacturers focus on the 
development of platform 
architecture, hardware components 
and software. The increased 
collaboration between OEMs and 
Tier-1 suppliers has resulted in the 
emergence of Tier 0.5 suppliers 
which take over responsibility for 
major systems and modules from a 
69 annual report  2024-2025chapter 13  global automotive industry
vehicle value creation perspective. 
Traditional automotive OEMs also 
utilise Tier-0.5 suppliers in various 
scenarios such as “JIT” (Just-in-Time) 
and “JIS” (Just-in-Sequence) 
processes given that suppliers are 
able to optimise production and 
processes with less uptime cost.
The recent supply chain disruptions 
and changing regulatory policies are 
resulting in OEMs to review sourcing 
strategies and recalibration of the 
production capacities. Motherson 
with its globally local manufacturing 
footprint and evolution from a “build-  
to-print” partner to an “advance 
technology partner” across the 
supply chain demonstrates our 
capacity to elevate our role to meet 
customer demands. Through the 
acquisition of SAS housed under 
Integrated Assembly, we have 
advanced into a Tier-0.5 supplier, 
managing complex supply chain 
operations with large opportunities 
to cross sell and scale up using  
our existing product portfolio and 
further develop our vertical

72chapter 13 global automotive industry
samvardhana motherson international limitedSustainability related drivers for 
clean mobility 
Global regulatory bodies and 
governments have intensified their 
focus on reducing carbon 
emissions, establishing various 
targets for carbon neutrality, as 
evidenced by the signing of the 
Paris Agreement by over 190 
countries. Various countries have 
set their own targets to facilitate the 
net zero transition, having the 
objective of minimising new petrol 
and diesel car sales. Below are 
some examples of regions and 
countries developing policies to 
facilitate carbon neutrality:
Europe: The most pronounced shift 
to electrification is expected in 
Europe, with strict restrictions on 
new ICE sales by 2035. The 
European Parliament in March 2023 
formally approved an EU Regulation 
to effectively ban the sale of new 
petrol and diesel cars in the EU from 
2035 as part of its climate 
protection plan "Fit for 55". This 
results in OEMs needing to achieve 
a 100% cut in CO2 emissions from 
new cars sold by 2035.
North America: Canada too has 
finalised legislation in 2023 setting 
the target of achieving 100% 
zero-emission vehicle sales by 
2035. The US, on the other hand, is 
experiencing a change in stance on 
EV-friendly legislation with the new 
administration taking office earlier 
this year. While some initiatives to 
lower emissions from vehicles in the 
USA remain, the current 
administration is rolling back and 
reviewing legislation initially 
designed to boost sales of low-
emission vehicles.SUV PremiumisationEurope

samvardhana motherson international limitedAutonomous and connected vehicles
Intelligent connectivity and digitisation, both inside and 
outside the vehicle, will play an ever more important 
role today and in the future. Vehicle to Vehicle 
Connectivity (V2x) is the name given to communication 
between one vehicle and another, and between a 
vehicle and the infrastructure, for instance with traffic 
lights or traffic control systems. Automated driving 
refers to the capability of a vehicle to drive itself at 
various levels of independence from the vehicle 
occupants to a destination in real world traffic, using its 
onboard sensors, and software intelligence, combined 
with navigation systems so that it can recognise its 
surroundings. 
The Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) defines 
6 levels of driving automation ranging from 0 (fully 
manual) to 5 (fully autonomous). Most public officials 
have strongly advocated for ADAS features to be 
included within the existing regulation, which has 
resulted in an increased penetration of ADAS 
functionality across all vehicle types. Although 
autonomous driving has made significant progress, 
especially in certain applications such as monorails, most 
personal vehicles currently adopt level-2, with level-3 
being the highest level of automation available to 
consumers today.
There are two significant barriers to ADAS adoption: 
regulation and consumer safety concerns. Various 
countries and each state in the US have their own sets 
of regulations around autonomous driving, which are 
being developed and enacted, adding further 
complexity for OEMs developing their autonomous 
driving systems and for consumer adoption.
As ADAS adoption grows, 
we support OEMs with 
smart, integrated safety 
solutions.

Samvardhana Motherson International Limited (SAMIL/ 
the Group) is a global powerhouse in design, 
engineering, manufacturing, and assembly, with over 
425 facilities (including all Operational Units, Tech 
Centres, and Representative Offices) across 44 
Countries and 5 Continents. Our global footprint, 
spanning both emerging and developing markets, 
enables us to support the evolving needs of our 
customers and anticipate upcoming industrial trends 
worldwide.
The year 2025 marks a significant milestone for the 
Group as it celebrates 50 years of operations since its 
founding in 1975. Starting with humble beginnings in 
India, the company has evolved from serving a single customer and offering a limited 
range of components to becoming 
a global powerhouse that provides 
sustainable solutions across diverse 
industries. Thanks to the trust 
placed in us by our customers, 
SAMIL is now the largest auto 
ancillary in India and ranks among 
the top 15 automotive suppliers 
worldwide.
SAMIL is listed on the BSE and 
National Stock Exchange (NSE) with 
a market capitalisation of USD 12.52 
billion as of July 14, 2025. The Motherson platform is based on 
three pillars of growth: (i) organic 
growth, (ii) strategic alliances with 
global technology leaders, and (iii) 
acquisitions. The robust, well-
diversified platform provides a 
strong foundation for existing 
businesses and incubates new 
ones, leveraging our core 
competencies in engineering and 
manufacturing while following 
prudent financial discipline.

five business segments, housing a 
well-diversified product portfolio, Samvardhana Motherson

Diversification: 3CX10 
diversification strategy is central to 
our resilient business model, 
enabling us to mitigate risks and 
maintain stability across economic 
cycles. By reducing dependency on 
specific customers, components, 
and countries, we effectively de-risk 
our operations. This approach also 
helps balance regional market 
fluctuations; ensuring that 
downturns in one market are offset 
by growth in others. This strategy 
not only makes our business model 
well diversified and resilient but also 
makes us a reliable partner to our 
customers over the long term. 
Further increasing content per OEM 
is aligned with our vision of 
providing sustainable solutions. 
Over this five-year period we have 
made significant progress in our 
diversification journey, (i) reducing 
dependence on any single 
customer to below 10% (ii) 
increasing penetration with 
Japanese OEMs, achieving 
empanelment as a Tier-1 supplier 
with an aerospace prime, Airbus, 
and gaining customers in the 
consumer electronics sector. Also, 
we were able to further diversify the 
component mix through the 
addition of (i) integrated assemblies 
business, (ii) an enhanced product 
portfolio through strategic 
acquisitions of Yachiyo and Dr. 
Schneider, and (iii) non-automotive 
growth via aerospace and 
consumer electronics. On the 
country front we are well positioned 
with a balanced exposure across 
emerging and developed markets.

ROCE: Return on Capital Employed 
(ROCE) remains a critical 
performance metric for Motherson, 
reflecting our commitment to 
capital efficiency and long-term 
value creation. Given the nature of 
our operations and our global 
presence across diverse 
geographies and industries, ROCE 
provides a comprehensive measure 
of how effectively we deploy 
financial resources to generate 
sustainable returns.As we pursue strategic growth initiatives, ROCE acts as 
a guiding benchmark, ensuring disciplined capital 
allocation and operational excellence. ROCE 
underscores our focus on profitable growth, financial 
prudence, and shareholder value enhancement. The 
Group's target of 40% applies to the entire organisation 
implying that every operating unit and business division 
should aspire to reach the 40% target. For Motherson, 
ROCE is a continuous journey as we continue to invest 
in future growth with new Greenfield and Brownfield 
expansions along with strategic acquisition. Therefore 
at an individual level some operating units and business 
divisions exceed the 40% target and for others it 
remains a work in progress.

Mergers & Acquisitions (M&A): 
These are a strategic enabler for Motherson's long-term 
growth journey. In an ever-evolving and extremely 
dynamic business environment, we are uniquely 
positioned as a strong trusted partner to our customers 
who seek resilient, and well capitalised players to 
strengthen and future proof the supply chain. Our 
approach is intentionally reactive and customer-
aligned, with opportunities typically emerging at the 
behest of our key partners. Each potential transaction is 
evaluated through a three-point alignment – between 
the customer, the target company, and Motherson to 
ensure strategic fit and long-term value creation. This 
disciplined approach allows us to focus on sustainable 
opportunities that enhance capabilities, foster 
operational integration, and unlock meaningful group 
synergies

•  Bonds USD 350 million: On July 3, 2024, SAMIL

the borrowing costs. The issuance is debt neutral as 
proceeds were used to repay existing debt. The notes 
are listed on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange.

strengthening the balance sheet.

material handling, and systems assembly. These 
facilities are equipped to support complex, high-volume 
production with scalable, modular, and efficient 
processes tailored to meet evolving customer 
requirements of various industries.
Through strategic investments in innovation, 
automation, and sustainability, and sharing of best 
practices and processes across all facilities, we are able 
to rapidly adapt, co-develop solutions, and ensure that 
we improve our products and deliver value added 
solutions on a global scale in a cost-efficient manner. 
This integrated, process-driven approach, combined 
with our ability to offer end-to-end system solutions, 
strong vertical integration, and in-house capabilities, 
enables us to consistently deliver operational excellence, 
adaptability, and long-term value to our global customers.
Our clear focus on the fundamentals of engineering 
and development is exemplified by the acronym 
QCDDMSES, which is our own measure that guides us 
in all aspects of our operations: (i) Quality - to ensure 
our quality standards meet the needs of our customers; 
(ii) Cost - to work to optimise cost levels; (iii) Design - to 
provide design support for current products and new concepts; (iv) Delivery -  
to deliver globally and follow our 
customers where they need us;  
(v) Management - to lead the 
organisation with the highest 
governance standards; (vi) Safety 
- to adhere to the highest standards 
of work safety; (vii) Environment - to 
adhere to the highest environmental 
standards; (viii) Sustainability – to be 
committed to long term rather than 
transactional relationships.

samvardhana motherson international limitedStrong performance driven by operational 
improvement
In the fiscal year ending March 31, 2025, the Wiring 
Harness Division delivered a solid performance, with  
a 4.27% year-on-year growth, reporting revenues of  
INR 328,610 million, compared to INR 315,137 million in 
the previous corresponding fiscal year ended March 31, 
2024. The growth is attributed to the following: (i) 
favourable content & model mix for medium-duty and 
heavy-duty trucks across key geographies of Europe 
and North America, despite a softening production 
environment offset by significant recovery in South 
America, primarily Brazil; (ii) sustained growth in India 
with new launches by marquee OEMs. The reported 
EBITDA increased to INR 38,729 million in the year 
ended March 31, 2025, registering a growth of 15.2% 
over the corresponding previous fiscal year. Despite 
operating in a challenging production environment 
marked by a sharp decline in the global commercial 
vehicle segment, the EBITDA margin improved by 110 
basis points to 11.8% in fiscal year 2025, from 10.7% in 
fiscal year 2024. This improvement was primarily due to 
stringent cost control measures, efforts to insource, and 
focused measures aimed at operational efficiencies.

automotive rearview mirrors and camera-based vision technologies. With 
a diverse portfolio ranging from high-performance camera monitoring 
systems and ADAS-driven technologies to advanced blind spot detection

products to leading automotive original equipment manufacturers (OEMs).  
Our offerings include cutting-edge front and rear exterior lighting systems, 
consumer electronics, LED modules, body control units, electronic 
components, HVAC systems, and aluminium die-cast parts. The division  
also caters to the independent aftermarket with auto suspension and brake 
components, wire harnesses, cabin filters, and a variety of car accessories.
By leveraging in-house product 
development, design validation, 
and manufacturing capabilities, the 
division offers OEMs a wide range 
of cutting-edge components that 
meet the growing demands for 
safety, connectivity, electrification, 
and energy efficiency across 
various vehicle platforms.
Performance overview
The Lighting & Electronics division 
delivered strong growth in FY2024–
25, with revenues rising to 
INR 40,779 million and EBITDA 
reaching INR 6,976 million. This 
reflects a more than two-fold 
increase in revenue over the last 
five years, significantly outpacing 
the growth of the Indian passenger 
vehicle market. The division’s 
performance was driven by 
increased content per vehicle – 
particularly in the  
SUV and EV segments, where  
we support customers with high-
technology, premium lighting systems – as well as by disciplined 
cost optimisation through better 
pricing, sourcing, and cross-
functional collaboration.
These results reaffirm the trust  
our customers have in our ability to 
deliver high-quality, high-volume 
solutions in technically demanding 
categories. With a strong order book, 
facilities equipped with advanced

focus on excellence, the division

Services .
The Services division comprises multiple businesses that offer  
direct sales and services to end customers while supporting their 
manufacturing and procurement activities. Its diverse portfolio 
includes an industrial park and services such as manufacturing and 
engineering consulting, project management, and turnkey solutions, 
as well as designing and manufacturing OEM-certified automotive 
parts, accessories, and dealer-fit products.
The division is also supported by two joint ventures: a 
partnership with Sojitz Corporation (Japan) for the 
development of the Sojitz Motherson Industrial Park 
(SMIP) in Chennai, and another with T-NET JAPAN Co., 
Ltd., which provides engineering and consulting services 
across both the automotive and non-automotive sectors.
Strong performance
The Services division delivered a standout performance 
in FY2024–25, with revenue rising to INR 14,503 million, 
representing a remarkable three-fold increase over the 
previous year (INR 4,953 million in FY2023–24). EBITDA 
also grew sharply from INR 138 million to INR 2,293 
million, driven by strong operational efficiency and 
improved cost discipline.
This growth was bolstered by both the successful 
integration of the Lumen Group and robust organic 
expansion. This acquisition expanded our product and 
engineering capabilities and opened access to new 
customer segments. We are now beginning to realise 
the full benefits of this acquisition, enabling us to deliver 
more comprehensive solutions, reach a broader market, 
and respond more effectively to customer needs. Product and capability 
expansion
The Services division made 
significant progress in FY2024–25 
by strengthening its ability to deliver 
faster and more customer-focused 
solutions. An important milestone 
was the integration of the Lumen 
Group, acquired in FY2023–24. This 
has added engineering, validation, 
and R&D expertise, particularly in 
genuine OEM accessories such as 
lighting systems, body electronics, 
harnesses, switches, and connectors. 
These additions have enabled us to 
provide more comprehensive and 
seamless solutions.
We also upgraded our facilities, 
adding advanced 3D scanning and 
printing systems in Australia. This 
new equipment speeds up in-house 
prototyping and reduces reliance 
on external suppliers. To keep up

we developed dedicated Controller Area Network (CAN) gateways. 
These ensure that our products are 
compatible with new vehicle wiring 
systems, improving efficiency and 
meeting OEM requirements. These 
efforts have enabled us to improve 
our speed to market and ensure we 
remain aligned with customer 
needs and industry trends.
The division achieved significant

Welcome to this year’s update on Motherson's 
sustainability journey. I am very pleased to be able to share 
with you an extensive amount of information through this 
report on the continued and meaningful progress we 
have made as we embed sustainability into every aspect 
of our operations and supply chain. 2024-2025 marked 
the conclusion of our 'Vision 2025' 5-year plan, providing 
an opportunity to reflect on our achievements, challenges, 
and the path ahead as we progress with our next strategy 
plan to 2030 and beyond. 
At the heart of our environmental strategy is a climate 
transition plan where we have a clear ambition: to achieve 
net zero emissions across our own operations (Scope 1 
and 2) by 2040. We are also working to address indirect 
emissions (Scope 3), particularly from purchased goods 
and services in our supply chain, which account for the 
majority of our overall carbon footprint. In accordance 
with the Paris Climate Agreement, we are committed to 
addressing this by 2050. Having such long-term strategic ambitions shapes behaviours in our 
daily working lives and ensures that 
sustainability is central to our 
business decisions. 
Over the past five years, Motherson 
has achieved remarkable growth, 
broadening and reinforcing its 
global presence while significantly 
expanding its facilities and 
workforce. With this growth comes 
a greater responsibility to our 
people, customers, investors, the 
communities in which we operate, 
and all our stakeholders. Throughout 
the organisation, we have deepened 
our commitment to sustainability, 
fostering greater awareness and 
understanding, to ensure it remains 
an integral part of how we do 
business. Our commitment remains 
unchanged: to be transparent 
about where we are and what 
progress we have made, be 
ambitious in what we want to 
achieve, and be accountable for 
our actions. As part of this, we 
continue to strengthen our 
approach to manage ESG risks  
and opportunities, aligning with 
the Task Force on Climate-related 
Financial Disclosures (TCFD), 
regarding climate transition 
scenarios. This helps us better 
understand the potential impact of 
climate change on our operations 
and enhances the transparency of 
our reporting. 
As we enter the next phase of our 
sustainability journey with the  
new Motherson 5-year plan, 'Vision 
2030’, we continue to work with 
passion to fulfill our vision of being 
a globally preferred sustainable 
solutions provider.
 
In this report, we highlight the 
tangible steps being taken to  
drive impact across environmental, 
social, and governance (ESG) 
dimensions. Sustainability is a 
collective effort, and with the 
engagement of all of our 
stakeholders, we continue to build 
a more resilient and responsible 
future.
